newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain's Socialists elect successor to Gonzalez.
newsitem.headline: Spain's Socialists elect successor to Gonzalez.

text.p: Veteran politician Joaquin Almunia was chosen on Sunday to replace his longtime ally, former Prime Minister Felipe Gonzalez, as head of Spain's Socialist Party.

Overcoming opposition from the party's left wing, Almunia -- a former cabinet minister who had worked for years in Gonzalez' shadow -- was elected to the top leadership role by an overwhelming majority of delegates at the Socialist congress.
"We have shown ourselves capable of launching a new phase," Almunia told cheering supporters. "Today is the start of a new future for Socialism in Spain."

The vote was the culmination of a fierce internal power struggle unleashed by Gonzalez' announcement Friday that he was stepping down as the party's secretary-general, a position he had held for most of the past 24 years.

Gonzalez, who steered Spain through an era of sweeping democratic renewal after nearly 40 years under dictator Francisco Franco, told the party faithful it was time for a "change of generations" in the Socialist hierarchy.
Almunia, 49, the party's parliamentary spokesman, quickly emerged as the top choice from a list of Socialist heavyweights that included regional presidents, national deputies and big city mayors.

But it was only after a night of tense, closed-door negotiations with the party's regional powerbrokers -- and a series of key concessions -- that Almunia won the backing needed to guarantee his election.

While party leaders sought to present a unified front, there were a few dissenting voices. Hard-line leftist delegates from three of the country's 17 autonomous regions -- Extremadura, Asturias and Cantabria -- were unhappy with Almunia's moderate stands and refused to support him.
And they made their opposition clear in the final vote count. Seventy-three percent of the delegates marked their ballots in favor of Almunia; 24.4 percent left theirs blank.

But most party members agree that Almunia has the skills needed to begin overhauling the Socialist Workers' Party, which was left demoralized after its defeat last year by the centre-right Popular Party led by Jose Maria Aznar.
The Socialist-leaning daily El Pais praised Almunia on Sunday as "a reformer who connects with the past."

The 55-year-old Gonzalez had promised not to interfere in the selection process and gave no hint of his preference for a successor. Nevertheless, the Socialists ended up picking one of his most stalwart loyalists.

That raised strong speculation that Gonzalez would keep controlling the party from behind the scenes and then make a dramatic comeback in time to lead the Socialists in the next general election scheduled for the year 2000.
Asked on Sunday whether he would run again, Gonzalez told reporters: "How can I answer that when it doesn't depend on me."

Even if Gonzalez does not return, some Socialist insiders believe Almunia -- considered more of a political technician than an inspiring leader -- will play only a "transitional" role and may never be given a chance to run for prime minister.
The clear favourite of the party's rank-and-file is NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana, who had taken himself out of the running this time around.

Solana, a former Socialist foreign minister, wants to see NATO through the first stage of its planned eastward expansion but has left open the possibility of returning to Spanish politics after his term ends in 1999, party sources said.
Born in the Basque port city of Bilbao, Almunia's party membership dates back to the mid-1970s when Gonzalez was still in exile trying to steer Spanish socialism away from its Marxist roots.

As Gonzalez rose in stature, Almunia moved up through the ranks and ever closer to his party's leader, winning election as a parliamentary deputy from Madrid in 1979. Gonzalez swept into power in 1982, and Almunia went on to serve as labour minister and later minister of public administration.
More recently as the party's parliamentary spokesman, he has steadily raised his public profile.
